facts.text: I asked to summarize an article about a U.S. Department of Justice investigation into Binance.
The article says the DOJ investigation into Binance began in 2018.
The article says the investigation focuses on Binance compliance with U.S. anti-money laundering laws and sanctions.
The article says some DOJ prosecutors believe evidence justifies filing criminal charges against Binance executives including founder Changpeng Zhao.
The article says other prosecutors argued for taking time to review more evidence before charging.

The article says the inquiry involves prosecutors at three DOJ offices: MLARS, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Washington in Seattle, and the National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team.
The article says DOJ regulations require money laundering charges against a financial institution to be approved by the MLARS chief.
The article says leaders from the other two offices and higher-level DOJ officials would likely also have to sign off on any action against Binance.
The article says Reuters pieced together the account through interviews with almost a dozen people familiar with the case and a review of company records.
The article says Binance defense attorneys at U.S. law firm Gibson Dunn held meetings with DOJ officials in recent months.
The article says the discussions included potential plea deals with Binance's attorneys.
The article says Binance spokesperson said Binance has no insight into the inner workings of the U.S. Justice Department and would not comment if it did.
The article says the Justice Department declined to comment.
The article says the charges under investigation include unlicensed money transmission, money laundering conspiracy, and criminal sanctions violations.
The article says no final charging decisions had been made at the time of the report.
The article says prosecutors considered Zhao and some other executives to be subjects of the investigation.
The article says the DOJ could bring indictments, negotiate a settlement, or close the case without taking action.

The article says Reuters previously reported that in 2020 prosecutors requested extensive internal records from Binance about anti-money laundering checks and communications involving Zhao and other executives.
The article says Zhao instigated a recruitment spree last year that led to hiring officials from the Internal Revenue Service's Criminal Investigation division.
The article says the article describes strict secrecy rules enforced by Zhao, including using email as little as possible and communicating using encrypted messaging services.
The article says Reuters investigated Binance's financial crime compliance over the course of 2022.

The article says Reuters reported Binance kept weak anti-money laundering controls, processed over $10 billion in payments for criminals and companies seeking to evade U.S. sanctions, and plotted to evade regulators in the United States and elsewhere.
The article says Binance disputed the articles, calling illicit-fund calculations inaccurate and compliance-control descriptions outdated.
The article says Binance said it is driving higher industry standards and seeking to further improve its ability to detect illegal crypto activity on its platform.
The article says Binance was launched by Zhao in Shanghai in 2017.
The article says Binance processed trades worth around $1.6 trillion in October, about half of the entire crypto market's trading volume.
The article says the article states FTX handled $230 billion in trades in October, according to CryptoCompare data.
The article says FTX imploded in early November.
The article says the Justice Department opened an investigation into FTX's handling of company funds.
The article says the article describes a bankruptcy hearing where attorneys for FTX said the exchange was run as a personal fiefdom of Sam Bankman-Fried.
The article says Sam Bankman-Fried said he didn't knowingly commit any wrongdoing.
The article says Zhao accelerated FTX's fall by announcing Binance would sell its holding of FTX's digital token.
The article says the article says this sparked a surge of user withdrawals and forced FTX to file for bankruptcy.
The article says Zhao wrote in a blog post several days later that Binance must lead by example going forward.
The article says Zhao wrote that Binance cannot let a few bad actors sully the reputation of the industry.
The article says prosecutors in the U.S. Attorney's Office in Seattle began investigating Binance in 2018.
The article says the Seattle office partnered with MLARS and agents from the IRS Criminal Investigation division to pursue the case.
The article says a company meeting summary in October 2018 attended by Zhao included the phrase "Lawyer up in the US, address regulatory risks."

The article says the U.S. Bank Secrecy Act requires crypto exchanges to register with the Treasury Department and comply with anti-money laundering requirements if they conduct substantial business in the United States.
The article says Binance has never registered with the Treasury Department despite almost a third of its users being U.S.-based the year of its launch.
The article says Zhao approved a proposal to insulate Binance from U.S. scrutiny by setting up a new American exchange that would draw regulators' attention away from the main platform.
The article says the article says Zhao became concerned about U.S. authorities gaining access to Binance's internal records.
The article says a guide issued to employees for an encrypted messaging service listed automatic self-erasing messages as a benefit.
The article says until 2020, Binance's legal department operated on bare bones and its head of legal was Jared Gross.
The article says the article says Binance hired an external lawyer from Paul Weiss, Roberto Gonzalez, in response to the Justice Department investigation.
The article says the article says Gonzalez was previously Treasury's deputy general counsel.
The article says the article says Gross left Binance last year.
The article says in December 2020, two MLARS attorneys and a Seattle prosecutor sent a DOJ request for documents to Binance addressed to Gonzalez.
The article says the December 2020 letter sought records containing instructions to destroy, alter, or remove documents or to not commit information to writing.
The article says the December 2020 request asked for communications involving Zhao and 12 other Binance executives and advisors.
The article says several days later an advisor to one of the people named in the letter received a panicked phone call about records already being erased due to Zhao's secrecy rules.
The article says the call extended to Zhao's approvals for financial decisions at Binance.US, the separate American exchange.
The article says Reuters reviewed text messages and phone records confirming the call took place and that it concerned the December 2020 letter.

The article says Binance.US spokesperson said Reuters' questions were fueled with false insinuations and that Binance.US is a separate entity with its own leadership team solely responsible for decisions and activity.
The article says Binance began a recruitment blitz the following year and hired at least five ex-officials from the IRS Criminal Investigation's Cyber Crime Unit.
The article says Binance hired Tigran Gambaryan as a new global head of investigations.
The article says Gambaryan was an IRS-CI special agent who helped lead investigations into the Silk Road darknet drugs marketplace and a child abuse site called Dark Scandals.
The article says Gambaryan was not involved in the Binance investigation at IRS-CI but was close to agents that were.
The article says Binance offered salaries that far exceeded what was available at many other finance and crypto firms as part of its recruitment program.
The article says Binance ended a policy in August 2021 that allowed users to open accounts with solely an email address.
The article says Reuters reported that criminals exploited the email-only account feature to move money anonymously through Binance.
The article says between August 2021 and November of the same year, Binance processed over $1 billion in trades for Iranian crypto firms.
The article says this put the company at risk of violating U.S. sanctions.
The article says in October 2021 Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco announced the creation of the National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team (NCET).
The article says the article says NCET was created to tackle investigations of criminal misuses of cryptocurrency, particularly crimes committed by virtual currency exchanges.
The article says the article says Lisa Monaco said the Justice Department's first priority in corporate criminal matters was to prosecute individuals who profit from corporate wrongdoing.
The article says the Justice Department appointed Eun Young Choi as NCET's first director.
The article says under Choi, NCET began coordinating the Binance investigation with the U.S. Attorney's Office in Seattle and MLARS.
The article says agents gathered evidence from former Binance employees and business partners.
The article says prosecutors at NCET and the Seattle office concluded they had sufficient evidence to prepare charges against Binance and Zhao and some other executives.
The article says MLARS leadership was hesitant to move forward with an indictment, causing frustrations within the investigation team.
The article says MLARS has a reputation for moving slowly in reaching prosecution decisions.
The article says in October the Department appointed a new MLARS chief, Brent Wible.
The article says Brent Wible previously worked in the Fraud Section and before that as a prosecutor in the Southern District of New York.
The article says Binance hired Kendall Day, a partner at Gibson Dunn and former chief of MLARS, to engage in discussions with the Justice Department.
The article says Kendall Day met with Justice officials in Washington in recent months.
The article says officials discussed a possible out-of-court resolution where suspects could plead guilty or pay a fine.

keyphrases: National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team director Eun Young Choi
